Hook: In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank was the sixteenth largest bank in America, banker to thousands of technology start-ups. On Wednesday the eighth it announced it had sold bonds at a loss and would raise new capital. On Thursday its customers withdrew forty-two billion dollars, in a single day, most of it from their phones. Overnight they asked for a hundred billion more, to be paid in the morning. On Friday morning the bank was closed by its regulator. About ninety-four percent of its deposits had been above the insured limit.

It did not stop at one bank. Here are deposits at America's small banks, week by week. In the week to the fifteenth of March they fell by about 149 billion dollars. Large banks gained about 54 billion. Depositors everywhere were asking which bank would be next. Two more failed that spring. The model that explains all of this was written forty years earlier, and it explains a run on a London bank in 1866 just as well.

This part's question: why are banks fragile, and can they be made safe? Why can a bank that has done nothing wrong fail when its depositors panic? What stops a run: suspending payments, insuring deposits, or a lender of last resort? And what does each of those cost?
Economics, Built. Part twenty-six: banks and runs.
A note before we start: this part explains how banks work and why they fail. It is not advice about any bank or any deposit.

Here is the plan. What a bank does, and a choice for you: stay, or withdraw? Then the model of 1983 that explains it, with its two equilibria. The three cures, and the moral hazard each creates. Capital, runs without any depositors at all, and a refinement that picks one equilibrium. And the evidence, what is lost when banks fail, two dials, the supervisors, and runs at the speed of a phone.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: stay, or withdraw?

Your turn. You have deposited one coconut at the Island's bank. If you withdraw tomorrow, the bank pays you 1.16. If you wait until its loans are repaid, it promises 1.42. You do not need the money tomorrow. But you hear a rumour: half of the other depositors will withdraw tomorrow. The bank will pay them in full, selling loans early if it has to. Do you stay, or withdraw? Pause, and choose.

Here is the arithmetic. A withdrawer gets 1.16, as long as the bank has anything left. A depositor who stays gets whatever is left when the loans are repaid, shared among the stayers. The more people withdraw, the more loans the bank sells early, and the less is left. If half withdraw, staying still gets you 1.26: if you chose A, you were right. But if more than about 59 percent withdraw, staying pays less than running. And if everyone believes everyone else will run, each is right to run. Nothing about the bank's loans has changed.
DD: Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig wrote the model in 1983; it won them a share of the Nobel prize in 2022. There are three dates, and each person starts with one unit. A share of them, here a quarter, will turn out to need their money early, at date one. The rest can wait. Nobody knows in advance which they will be, and nobody can prove their type to anyone else. The only investment pays 1.5 if it is held to date two, but only one if it is cut short. On their own, people get one if they turn out impatient, and one and a half if patient. That is a gamble on their own type, and people who dislike risk would pay to insure it.

A bank can provide that insurance. Choose what to pay at each date to maximize expected utility, given that whatever is paid early must come from investments cut short. The first-order condition says the marginal utility of early consumption equals R times that of late. With constant relative risk aversion, the solution is in closed form. With a risk aversion of two, the bank pays 1.16 to anyone who withdraws early and 1.42 to anyone who waits: more than one for the impatient, less than one and a half for the patient. That is a demand deposit. It makes everyone better off, provided only the impatient withdraw early. And that proviso is the whole problem.
Run: Chapter four. Two equilibria: the bank and the run.

Write down what a patient depositor gets. If everyone else waits, waiting pays 1.42, and withdrawing only 1.16: so wait. That is the good equilibrium. If everyone else runs, the bank must sell every loan at one to pay 1.16 each, and it can pay only 86 percent of the queue. Those who wait get nothing. So run. Both are equilibria. The same bank, with the same loans, is sound if people believe it is, and fails if they believe it will.

The run is made worse by a rule of banking: first come, first served. In a run, the bank pays 1.16 to each depositor in the order they arrive, until the money runs out. On the Island, 862 of 1000 depositors are paid in full and the rest get nothing. So being early is everything, and waiting to see what happens is the worst thing you can do. That is why a run, once it starts, is fast.

What decides which one happens? In the model, nothing about the bank: any event people treat as a signal will do. Economists call it a sunspot. In life: a rumour, a queue outside a branch, a falling share price, a post that spreads. So runs can hit sound banks. But weak banks are more exposed, because less bad news is needed to tip them over. Chapter ten shows how a refinement of the model picks one equilibrium after all.
Cures: Chapter five. Suspension and deposit insurance.

Diamond and Dybvig also showed how to remove the bad equilibrium. The first cure is to suspend convertibility: announce that once a quarter of the depositors have withdrawn, the share who are truly impatient, the bank will pay nothing more until the loans come due. Then a patient depositor who waits is sure of 1.42, more than the 1.16 that running brings. So nobody runs, and the suspension never has to be used. But it works only if the bank knows how many people genuinely need their money. If that number is uncertain, suspending can lock out people who need cash, which is what happened in the American panics of the nineteenth century.

The second cure is deposit insurance. The government promises every insured depositor full payment, whatever happens to the bank. Then no depositor has any reason to run, so the bank is never run. And here is the remarkable part: in the model, insurance against runs is never paid out, so it costs nothing. The promise alone removes the bad equilibrium. As long as people believe it, which requires a government that could raise the money if it ever had to.

The cure has been tried. Here are American commercial banks suspended each year from 1921 to 1941. From 1930 to 1933, about 8,812 banks failed or closed their doors. In 1933 alone, 3,891. Federal deposit insurance began on the first of January 1934. That year, 44 banks were suspended. Other things changed in 1933 too, from the banking holiday to the end of the gold standard, but bank runs largely disappeared from America for the next seventy years.
Bagehot: Chapter six. Bagehot's rule: the lender of last resort.

The third cure is older. In May 1866, Overend, Gurney and Company, the biggest discount house in London, failed. The next day, remembered as Black Friday, depositors ran on banks across the City. The Bank of England lent heavily to anyone who could offer good security, and the panic subsided. Walter Bagehot, the editor of The Economist, turned that into a rule in his book Lombard Street, in 1873.

Bagehot's rule has three parts, as it is usually summarized. In a panic, the central bank should lend freely, without limit, so that nobody needs to run for fear of being last. At a penalty rate, so that only banks that need the money borrow it, and repay as soon as they can. And against good collateral: to banks that are illiquid, short of cash but sound, not to banks that are insolvent. The hard part, every time, is telling the two apart in the middle of a panic.

Agora makes the point with numbers. A sound bank holds ten in reserves and ninety in loans, against ninety of deposits and ten of equity. In a panic, depositors withdraw 30, twenty more than its reserves. With no lender, it must sell loans in a hurry, at sixty percent of their value: 33 of loans to raise twenty, and its equity falls to -3.3. It is insolvent. With Bagehot's lender, it borrows twenty against its loans at a penalty rate of five percent, and its equity is 9. The fire sale is what kills it: it turns a shortage of cash into a hole in the balance sheet.
Hazard: Chapter seven. The price: moral hazard.

Every cure has a price. Robert Merton showed in 1977 how to value deposit insurance. Take a bank with assets of 100 and insured deposits of 90, so the owners' own money, the dashed line, is 10. The insurer pays depositors whatever the assets fall short of a year from now. That is a put option on the bank's assets, and its value, in pink, rises steeply with how risky those assets are. In green, the value of the owners' stake. With assets as volatile as a quarter of their value in a year, the put is worth 5.3, and the owners' stake is worth 15.3, not 10. If the premium is flat, every dollar of the insurer's expected loss is a dollar for the owners. So insurance rewards the bank for taking risks, unless it is priced to the risk, capped, or matched by rules. Depositors who never run also never watch.

America learned this the expensive way. In the 1980s, the savings and loan associations held long, fixed-rate mortgages, funded by insured deposits. When interest rates jumped, many became insolvent. Allowed to keep operating, some gambled on risky loans: if the bets paid off, the owners recovered; if not, the insurer paid. The clean-up cost taxpayers as much as a hundred and twenty-four billion dollars. The same logic applies to banks so large that creditors expect a rescue: they can borrow more cheaply, and grow larger. Part thirty-three returns to too big to fail.
Capital: The other answer to moral hazard is capital: make the owners put in money of their own, which is lost first. In 1988, American banks' equity was about 6 percent of their assets. By 2020 it was about 10. Equity absorbs losses before depositors or the insurer lose anything. Even so, about nine dollars in ten of what a bank owns is financed by borrowing.

Capital rules count risk. Each asset gets a weight, and capital is measured against the weighted total. Government bonds have no credit risk, so they get a weight of zero, and the Island's bank looks well capitalized: 17 percent of risk-weighted assets. But government bonds have interest-rate risk. If rates rise three points, its ten-year bonds lose 24 percent of their value. That is a loss of 7.1, leaving equity of 2.9: 3 percent of its assets. Silicon Valley Bank ended 2022 with 91 billion dollars of bonds it planned to hold to maturity, worth about 15 billion less than their book value, while its reported capital ratio was 12 percent. The loss was real only if it had to sell. A run makes you sell.

How much capital, then? Banks argue that equity is expensive, so requiring more of it means less lending. Anat Admati and Martin Hellwig argued in 2013 that equity is expensive for banks mainly because their debt is subsidized, by insurance and expected rescues, and proposed equity of twenty to thirty percent of total assets. Their argument is Modigliani and Miller's, from Part twenty-three: more equity makes each share safer, so the return shareholders require falls. Today's rules require much less than their number, and the argument continues.
Shadow: By 2007, much of America's lending no longer ran through deposits at all. Here is a dealer bank holding 100 of securities, funded by 4 of its own money and 96 of repo. A repo is a sale of a bond today with a promise to buy it back tomorrow at a slightly higher price. In effect it is an overnight loan, secured by the bond, rolled over every day. The lender keeps a margin, called the haircut: it lends only 96 against a bond worth a hundred. And the lenders are money market funds, companies' treasurers and other banks, with no deposit insurance behind them. Gary Gorton and Andrew Metrick argued that this is where the run of 2007 and 2008 happened.

A run on repo does not look like a queue. It looks like a number. If lenders keep a haircut h, a dealer can hold at most its equity divided by h. At a haircut of 4 percent, that is 25 times its equity. In 2007 and 2008, lenders worried about what the bonds were worth and raised haircuts. At 20 percent, the most it can hold is 5 times its equity. So with the same 4 of equity, the dealer can now carry only 20 of securities, and must sell 80, into a market where everyone else is selling too. Raising the haircut is withdrawing the deposit. Gorton and Metrick's data covered only some kinds of collateral, and critics argue the run was smaller in the wider repo market; that it happened in securitized bonds is not in doubt.

Money market funds took deposits in all but name: shares meant to be worth exactly one dollar, which you could withdraw at any time. On the sixteenth of September 2008, the day after Lehman Brothers failed, the oldest of them, the Reserve Primary Fund, broke the buck. It held seven hundred and eighty-five million dollars of Lehman's short-term paper, about one percent of the fund, and its shares were marked down to ninety-seven cents. By that afternoon, investors had asked for about a quarter of the fund's money. On the nineteenth, the Treasury guaranteed money funds' shares. Here is the strange part: money funds' total assets rose that autumn, from 3.4 to 3.8 trillion dollars. The money did not leave the funds. It left the prime funds, which lend to companies, for funds that hold only government debt. The run was on companies' short-term borrowing. In March 2020, prime funds ran again, and the Federal Reserve set up a facility to lend against their assets.

The lesson. Shadow banking is maturity transformation outside the banks. It is funded short, by repo, commercial paper and money-fund shares, all of which can run. It holds long or illiquid assets: mortgage bonds and loans to companies. It had no deposit insurance, and in 2007 no lender of last resort. In 2008, the Federal Reserve lent to dealers and money funds directly, and in effect became one. Diamond and Dybvig's model fits wherever there is short funding and long assets.
Global: Chapter ten. One equilibrium after all: global games.

Diamond and Dybvig leave a hole. With two equilibria, the model says a run can happen, but not when, or how likely it is. In 1998, Stephen Morris and Hyun Song Shin found a way to close it, first for currency attacks. Give each player a slightly different view of the fundamentals. Say the bank has a strength theta, and fails if the share of depositors withdrawing reaches theta. Each depositor sees theta plus a little private noise. Nobody knows exactly what the others see. Then, however small the noise, there is only one equilibrium: withdraw if and only if your signal is below a cutoff.

Here is the Island's version. Across the bottom, the bank's strength. Up the side, the share of depositors who withdraw. The dashed line is where the share withdrawing equals the strength: above it, the bank fails. A depositor who withdraws gets 1. One who stays gets 2 if the bank survives and nothing if it fails. In red, the share withdrawing in the unique equilibrium, simulated with 2,000 depositors. When the bank is weak, almost everyone runs; when it is strong, almost nobody does; the switch is sharp. And the bank fails exactly when its strength is below 0.5, the ratio of what withdrawing pays to what staying pays. A bank that would have survived if everyone stayed still fails, if it is weak enough: the run is real, but it is now predictable.

Why that ratio? Put yourself at the cutoff. You are indifferent: staying pays R times the chance the bank survives, and that must equal c. At the cutoff you cannot tell whether your signal is high or low compared with everyone else's, so every share of depositors below you is equally likely. Morris and Shin call this belief Laplacian. The bank survives if its strength exceeds the share withdrawing, so your chance of survival is theta star itself, and theta star is c over R. The noise only has to be there; how large it is drops out of the answer.

The unique equilibrium lets us ask a question the old model could not. With a deposit that pays 1 on demand, the bank fails when its strength is below 0.5. Make the deposit more generous to people who withdraw early, 1.2 instead of 1, and it fails below 0.6. The yellow band is the extra failures. Better insurance for the impatient makes running more attractive, so runs become more likely. Itay Goldstein and Ady Pauzner worked this out for Diamond and Dybvig's bank in 2005: the best deposit contract trades risk sharing against the probability of a run, and it offers less than the contract that ignores runs.
Evidence: Chapter eleven. Runs in the data.

Were the runs of the Great Depression panics, sunspots in Diamond and Dybvig's sense, or were bad banks simply found out? Here are American bank suspensions month by month, from 1929 to February 1933. Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz picked out four banking crises. The first came at the end of 1930, when the Bank of United States, a large New York bank, closed in December. The second in the spring and summer of 1931. The third after Britain left the gold standard in September 1931: 522 banks were suspended in October alone. And the last in early 1933, which ended with every bank in the country closed by the banking holiday of March.

Charles Calomiris and Joseph Mason tested the question bank by bank. They built a model of each Federal Reserve member bank's risk of failing, from its own balance sheet and the state of its county's economy. Then they looked for failures the fundamentals could not explain. In the crises of 1930 and the spring of 1931, they found none: banks failed when their fundamentals said they would. In the autumn of 1931 the evidence is ambiguous, and the unexplained part is small. In early 1933 there was a large unexplained rise in failures: a panic. So, mostly, weak banks were found out, with some contagion between neighbouring banks, until the very end. Fundamentals and runs work together, as the global game says they should.

In 2023 the same question came back. Erica Jiang, Gregor Matvos, Tomasz Piskorski and Amit Seru valued the assets of every American bank at market prices. After the rate rises of 2022, those assets were worth about two trillion dollars less than their book value, about ten percent on average. A loss like that need not sink a bank whose depositors are insured, because they have no reason to run. It matters when uninsured depositors can leave. If only half of the uninsured withdrew, they estimated, about a hundred and ninety banks, with about three hundred billion dollars of assets, could be left unable to pay everyone. Silicon Valley Bank had large losses, and 94 percent of its deposits uninsured. Weak fundamentals made the run possible; the uninsured made it happen.
Monitors: Douglas Diamond asked a more basic question in 1984. Why lend through a bank at all? Suppose a firm needs money from a thousand savers, and checking on what the firm does with it costs each of them a little. If every saver checks, the checking is done a thousand times. If nobody checks, nobody is watching, and the firm can claim it did badly and pay little. Delegate the checking to a bank, and it is done once. But then the savers have a new problem: who watches the bank?

Diamond's answer is diversification. On the Island, each loan repays 1.3 with probability 0.9 and nothing otherwise, and the bank promises its depositors one for every loan. With a single loan, the bank fails to pay them one time in ten. With ten loans, about 7 percent of the time. With a hundred, about four times in a hundred thousand. A bank with many independent loans can promise a fixed payment and nearly always keep it, so its depositors hardly need to watch it. That is why a bank's liabilities are simple debts. The catch is the word independent: in a crisis, loans go bad together.

If banks exist to know their borrowers, a bank failure destroys something. That was Ben Bernanke's argument in 1983. What a bank knows about its borrowers is a kind of capital, built up over years of lending, and it dies with the bank. When thousands of banks failed from 1930 to 1933, farmers, households and small firms lost credit that no other lender knew them well enough to give. In his regressions, the failures help explain the collapse of output, beyond what the fall in the money supply explains. In 2022, Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig shared the Nobel prize for their research on banks and financial crises.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: deposit betas, and the cost of a crisis.

Two dials open in this part. The first is the deposit beta: the share of a rise in the policy rate that banks pass on to their depositors. Economists at the New York Fed found that in the tightening of 2004 to 2006, the beta on interest-bearing deposits approached sixty percent by the end. In the cycle of 2015 to 2019 it never passed forty. In the much faster tightening of 2022 it reached almost forty percent by the end of the year. S&P Global's figure for all deposits, by the third quarter of 2023, was thirty-eight and a half. This film's own, from the FDIC's national rates: savings accounts passed on 8 percent of the rise, twelve-month certificates of deposit 33. The status: it depends on the setting, the product, and how long the rise has lasted. And a low beta is worth something to a bank only while its depositors stay.

The second dial: how much output a banking crisis costs. Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff found that after systemic banking crises, real output per person fell by more than nine percent from peak to trough, on average. Valerie Cerra and Sweta Saxena, with data on a hundred and ninety countries, found that the loss after a banking crisis is about ten percent and does not go away. Christina and David Romer, measuring financial distress directly in twenty-four rich countries, found a peak decline nearer six percent, and only four in another specification, and very different from one crisis to the next. America in 2008: real GDP fell 3.8 percent from peak to trough. But by 2019 it was 18 percent below the trend of 1990 to 2007, which would be the biggest number here, if that trend was the right one to draw; growth had begun to slow before the crisis. The status: contested. The cost is large, but how large depends on what you compare it with.
Practice: Chapter fourteen. In practice: stress tests, the treasury desk, deposit pricing.

Since the first stress test, in 2009, America's largest banks have had to show regularly that they could survive a severe recession, described by the Federal Reserve in a scenario. The scenario published in February 2022 had the ten-year Treasury yield falling to three quarters of a percent, short-term rates near zero throughout, and unemployment rising to ten percent. That is what severe recessions had looked like before. What happened instead: the ten-year yield rose from 1.8 percent to about 4 percent by October. And the federal funds rate went from almost nothing to 4.1 percent within the year.

Called it? A stress scenario is not a forecast, and the Federal Reserve says so. But it is a judgment about which dangers matter, and in 2022 the danger it tested was a recession with falling rates. The danger that arrived was rising rates. The losses that sank Silicon Valley Bank came from long bonds losing value as yields rose, a risk the scenario did not test; and Silicon Valley Bank, grown large only recently, was not yet among the banks being tested. Wrong, as a judgment of where the danger was. Since 2023 the Federal Reserve has added exploratory analyses, with other kinds of shock, beside the main test.

Deposit pricing is a bank's daily decision. From February 2022 to December 2023, the federal funds rate rose from 0.08 to 5.33 percent. The national average rate on twelve-month certificates of deposit rose to 1.86 percent: a beta of a third. On savings accounts, to 0.46 percent: a beta under a tenth. The gap is what depositors pay the bank for convenience, and for not shopping around. Itamar Drechsler, Alexi Savov and Philipp Schnabl call it the deposit franchise, and showed that it works like a hedge: when rates rise, a bank's long assets lose value, but its sticky deposits become more valuable. That hedge holds only if the depositors stay.

And the treasury desk, which manages the whole balance sheet. Its first number is duration. A ten-year bond yielding one and a half percent has a duration of 9.2 years: each point on yields costs about 9 percent of its price. Against long assets it sets deposits, which may stay for years, or leave in a day. Since Basel III, large banks must hold enough liquid assets to cover thirty days of outflows in a stress. And a good desk knows in advance what it can pledge at the central bank's discount window, and has tested it. In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank faced thirty days of stressed outflows in a single day.
Frontier: Chapter fifteen. Frontier: digital runs, narrow banks, stablecoins.

The frontier begins with speed. Silicon Valley Bank lost 42 billion dollars in one day, and was asked for 100 billion more overnight. A run used to need a queue on the pavement. Now it needs a phone. And a crowd that talks: the bank's depositors were start-up founders and their investors, many of them connected on social media. Anthony Cookson and his coauthors found that banks that had been discussed most on Twitter before the run lost more of their stock-market value during it, beyond what their unrealized losses and uninsured deposits would predict. Diamond and Dybvig's depositors coordinate on a sunspot; these ones could watch each other do it.

The response came on Sunday the twelfth of March. The Treasury, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC announced that every depositor of Silicon Valley Bank and of Signature Bank, insured or not, would be paid in full. And the Federal Reserve opened a new programme lending to banks for up to a year against Treasury and agency bonds, valued not at their market price but at par. That goes beyond Bagehot. He asked for collateral that would be good in ordinary times, valued as it would be without the panic. These bonds had lost value because interest rates had risen, not because of the panic. The run stopped. What the weekend promised for the next run, every uninsured depositor could work out.

Could money be made unrunnable? That is the idea of narrow banking. In 1933 a group of Chicago economists proposed it, and in 1935 Irving Fisher made the case in a book called One Hundred Percent Money: back every deposit one for one with reserves at the central bank. Lending would then be financed by equity and long-term debt, which cannot run. The objection has always been that the maturity transformation would not disappear. It would move outside the banks, into the shadows of chapter nine. A stablecoin backed by Treasury bills is a narrow bank outside the law of banks, and it can still be run. On Friday the tenth of March 2023, Circle disclosed that three point three billion dollars of the reserves behind its coin, USDC, were at Silicon Valley Bank. Over the weekend the coin fell to about eighty-eight cents, and recovered its dollar only when the depositors were protected.

The questions still open. Should deposit insurance cover companies' payroll accounts in full, since in practice it did? If a run can take hours, must the lender of last resort be ready at any hour, with collateral already pledged? How much capital should banks hold, and should the bonds they plan to keep be counted at market prices? And can stablecoins and tokenized deposits be made safe without becoming banks, with everything that comes with that?
